channel.title: HAT MI Daily - Macro and Industries
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The European Commission plans to withdraw the proposed EU regulation against late payment, which would have sanctioned companies that pay suppliers late, in its 2027 Work Programme, La Vanguardia reports.
item.description:
The European Commission has decided to include the proposed Regulation against Late Payment among the legislative initiatives it plans to withdraw in its Work Programme for 2027, La Vanguardia reports. According to the report, pressure from the Council (named in the report as the Council of Europe), particularly from Germany, will prevent companies that pay their suppliers late from being sanctioned, as the European Parliament had approved. The SME business association Pimec, which had promoted the regulation with other SME employers' associations, said Europe is giving in to large business lobbies and that the withdrawal would leave nearly 34 million companies, mostly SMEs and self-employed, unprotected, at a time of worsening payment terms, high interest rates and high inflation. The row does not give the regulation's provisions beyond sanctions, a date for the withdrawal or the Commission's reasons.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a withdrawal planned in the 2027 Work Programme, not a completed one. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, dropping the regulation, including sanctions for late payers, leaves payment terms in the EU to contracts and existing rules, which favours large buyers in negotiations with smaller suppliers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, suppliers sell both to large industrial customers, where payment terms affect their own receivables, and to small trade and construction customers, whose payment behaviour affects their credit risk. Points that may be worth considering include the final Work Programme, the reaction of member states and the Parliament, and payment-term trends in the construction and manufacturing supply chains.

La Vanguardia

item.title: The White House announced a framework for a reciprocal trade agreement with Thailand on 17 November, under which Thailand would eliminate tariffs on 99% of US goods and buy US farm products, and Trump said non-tariff barriers on US cars would also fall.
item.description:
The White House announced a framework for an agreement on reciprocal trade with Thailand on 17 November, the U.S. Grains Council reports. Under the proposed agreement Thailand would eliminate tariffs on 99% of US goods, including agricultural products, begin issuing import permits for US ethanol and buy USD 2.6 billion in US agricultural products a year, including corn and distillers' dried grains. President Trump said Thailand will significantly reduce non-tariff barriers on US automobiles, medical equipment, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry and abolish tariffs on all US exports, Commercial Times reports, and that the agreement is expected to be finalised in the coming weeks, MarketScreener reports. The US is Thailand's largest export market, taking 24.6% of its exports so far in 2026, and the two countries had announced a preliminary framework in October 2025 under which Thailand would eliminate tariffs on about 99% of US goods, MarketScreener reports. The rows do not give US tariff rates on Thai goods or a signing date.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a framework announced by the US side, not a signed agreement, and give two descriptions of its scope, 99% of goods and all exports. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, lower Thai tariffs and non-tariff barriers favour US exporters of cars, medical equipment and pharmaceuticals in Thailand, and the deal's value for Thailand depends on the US tariff on Thai goods, which the rows do not give. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Thailand is a vehicle and electronics production base, so the terms for car imports and for Thai exports to the US bear on production there and on demand from its manufacturers. Points that may be worth considering include the signed text, the US tariff on Thai goods and the treatment of cars and parts.

U.S. Grains Council | Commercial Times | MarketScreener

item.title: Indian construction equipment sales are expected to reach 126,500 to 133,500 units in the 2026/27 fiscal year, with demand strengthening in the second half, the industry association ICEMA says.
item.description:
The Indian Construction Equipment Manufacturers' Association (ICEMA) expects sales of construction equipment to reach 126,500 to 133,500 units in the 2026/27 fiscal year, The Economic Times reports. It expects demand to strengthen in the second half, led by earthmoving equipment, because of the resumption of mining activity, a pick-up in building and industrial construction, favourable input costs and the seasonally strong year-end construction cycle. Infrastructure capital expenditure is expected to increase significantly over the coming years, and road construction equipment sales are projected to stay stable despite a decline in highway construction. The row does not give sales for the first half or for the previous fiscal year, so the expected change cannot be calculated.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row is an industry forecast, not measured sales. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, an expected pick-up in building and industrial construction, with highway building declining, points to a shift in India's construction mix from roads towards buildings and industrial sites. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, building and industrial construction use more flooring, sealing, insulation and installation products than road building, and equipment manufacturing itself uses bonding and sealing materials. Points that may be worth considering include ICEMA's half-year sales figures, Indian cement and steel demand, and infrastructure spending in the coming budget.

The Economic Times

item.title: Türkiye's housing price index rose 0.7% in October from September and 21.1% year on year, a fall of 6.6% in real terms, central bank data show.
item.description:
According to the Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye, the Housing Price Index rose 0.7% in October 2026 from September to 240.9, Dünya reports. Housing prices rose 21.1% year on year but fell 6.6% when adjusted for inflation. Rents for new tenants rose 24.5% year on year, a real decline of 4.1%, and 0.1% from September. Istanbul recorded the largest annual increases in housing prices and rents among the three largest cities. The row does not give housing sales, construction permits or starts.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives prices, not construction volumes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, house prices and new-tenant rents both falling in real terms point to weak real demand in a high-inflation economy, which usually limits new residential building beyond projects already under way. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Turkish residential construction and renovation use tile, flooring, sealing and insulation products, and with prices rising more slowly than inflation, demand is more likely to come from renovation and maintenance than from new building. Points that may be worth considering include Turkish housing sales and building permits, and the path of inflation and interest rates.

Dünya

item.title: The NAHB/Wells Fargo index of US home builder confidence fell to 25 in November, its lowest in 14 years, with 46% of builders cutting prices and 68% offering sales incentives, both post-Covid highs.
item.description:
The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index, a gauge of builder confidence in the market for newly built single-family homes, decreased to 25 in November, its lowest level in 14 years, MarketScreener reports. A reading below 50 means builders' views of current sales and sales expectations are net negative. High mortgage rates, ongoing inflation pressure, elevated energy and material costs, rising labour shortages and hesitant buyers weighed on confidence. In November 46% of builders reduced prices, the highest share in the post-Covid period, and the average price reduction held at 6% for an eighth straight month. 68% of builders offered sales incentives, also a post-Covid high. The row does not give the October reading, housing starts or permits.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The index measures builder sentiment, not construction activity. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, the highest post-Covid shares of builders cutting prices and offering incentives indicate that builders are selling homes already planned or built at lower margins, and weak confidence tends to reach new construction starts with a delay. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, US single-family construction uses flooring, sealing, insulation and installation products, so lower starts would reduce demand in these segments, while builders under margin pressure may look for cheaper materials or faster application. Points that may be worth considering include November housing starts and permits, mortgage rates and the December Fed decision.

MarketScreener

item.title: The US is adding Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and, in most reports, Brazil to its advanced-chip export-licence list, with customer checks for data-centre operators, and data-centre and chip shares fell in Asia.
item.description:
The US Commerce Department has added Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Singapore to a list of countries for which shipments of advanced chips made by Nvidia and other US companies will require export licences, MarketScreener reports; Wirtschaftswoche and a later MarketScreener report also name Brazil, and Commercial Times reports that the regulation lists Brazil among countries where advanced chips are at higher risk of being resold to China. The aim is to curb Chinese customers' access to computing capacity in other countries and to prevent smuggling to China, and new customer verification requirements were introduced for data-centre operators using US AI chips, Wirtschaftswoche reports. LiveMint reports that the rule imposes new requirements on overseas data centres that supply significant volumes of computing power to companies headquartered in China, and that on 17 November shares of data-centre and chip supply chain companies in Southeast Asia fell, with the selloff spreading to data-centre material suppliers and printed circuit board, thermal management and energy stocks in China, South Korea, Japan and Taiwan. According to Chris Hampden of Proxima, part of Bain & Co., procuring and deploying advanced AI infrastructure could become more complex, increasing operating costs and lengthening investment decisions, MarketScreener reports. The rows do not give the chip thresholds, the date licences become required or how licences will be granted.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a licence requirement and a market reaction, not changes in shipments. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a licence requirement for the region's major economies adds time and uncertainty to projects there and may move some AI computing capacity to locations with fewer restrictions. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, data-centre construction, server and circuit board assembly and thermal management use adhesive, sealing and thermal interface materials, so where data-centre capacity is built affects where this demand arises in Asia. Points that may be worth considering include licence decisions, project announcements in Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, and the outcome of the 19 November Trump–Xi–Putin meeting in Shenzhen.

MarketScreener | Wirtschaftswoche | LiveMint | MarketScreener | Commercial Times

item.title: Italian new car registrations rose 4.8% year on year to 131,921 in October and 8.3% in January–October, and UNRAE raised its 2026 estimate to 1.64 million cars, while light commercial vehicle registrations fell 10.1% in October.
item.description:
Italy recorded 131,921 new car registrations in October 2026, 4.8% more than the 125,864 a year earlier, ANSA reports. Registrations in January to October reached 1,400,991, up 8.3% on the same period of 2025, but over 224,000 or 13.8% below the same period of 2019. Citing a better macroeconomic and consumer spending outlook, UNRAE raised its 2026 estimate to 1,640,000 cars, 7.5% more than in 2025 but 14.4% below 2019, and expects volumes to fall 3.4% to 1,585,000 in 2027. The Italian market for light commercial vehicles up to 3.5 tonnes fell 10.1% year on year in October to 15,574 units and 5.4% in the first ten months to 150,445, Il Gazzettino reports. The rows do not give the split by powertrain or brand.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows give registrations, which measure sales in Italy, not where the cars are built. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a car market still well below 2019 with a decline expected in 2027 suggests the 2026 recovery is not a new trend, and falling van registrations point to weaker business investment in transport. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, demand from the automotive industry follows vehicle production more than sales in one country, so Italian registrations matter mainly as a signal of European car demand. Points that may be worth considering include European registrations from ACEA, the powertrain mix and Italian vehicle production.

ANSA | Il Gazzettino

item.title: US production of motor vehicles and parts rose 4.4% in October and manufacturing output 0.3%, above the 0.2% expected, with AI-related segments also up, while total industrial output fell 0.4%, Federal Reserve data show.
item.description:
US manufacturing output increased 0.3% in October 2026, slightly more than the 0.2% economists expected, according to Federal Reserve data reported by MarketScreener. Growth was driven by a 4.4% increase in production of motor vehicles and parts and by segments linked to the build-out of artificial intelligence infrastructure: semiconductors and related electronic components rose 2.2%, computers and peripheral equipment 3.2% and communications equipment 0.9%. Durable goods production grew 0.5%. Mining production declined 0.8%, and utilities output fell 4.3% because of lower demand for heating. Overall industrial output fell 0.4% in the month but rose 2.1% year on year. The row does not give the year-on-year change for manufacturing or for vehicles.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives monthly changes in production volumes by industry. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, growth concentrated in vehicles and AI-related electronics, with total industrial output lower as mining and utilities fell, describes a narrow manufacturing expansion rather than a broad one. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle, electronics and computer assembly are among the main industrial users of bonding, sealing and thermal management materials, so the segments that grew are ones where these products are used. Points that may be worth considering include November production data, vehicle output trends and capacity utilisation.

MarketScreener

item.title: The European Commission raised its 2026 growth forecast for Germany to 1.3%, from 0.6% in May, and for the EU to 1.4%, cut France to 0.4% and expects eurozone inflation of 3.2% this year.
item.description:
The European Commission expects the German economy to grow 1.3% in 2026, after several years of stagnation, Süddeutsche Zeitung reports; the Commission published its Autumn 2026 Economic Forecast on 17 November, People's Daily reports. In May the Commission had cut its projection to 0.6% because of high energy prices resulting from the Iran war; the increase is attributed mainly to a strong rise in exports at the start of the year. For Germany it expects growth to fall gradually to 0.7% by 2028, and its 2026 and 2027 forecasts match those of the German Council of Economic Experts, Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports. EU growth is projected at 1.4% in 2026 and 2027 and 1.5% in 2028, according to People's Daily, and eurozone growth at 1.2% in 2026, up from 0.9% projected in May, and in 2027, MarketScreener reports. France's 2026 forecast was cut from 0.8% to 0.4%, Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports, and MarketScreener reports 0.6% in 2027, the weakest growth in the eurozone. Eurozone inflation is projected to jump to 3.2% in 2026 from 2.1% in 2025 and to ease only to 3.1% in 2027. The rows do not give an earlier EU forecast, a sector breakdown, German inflation or the investment outlook.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

These are forecasts, not measured output, and the German upgrade rests on exports early in the year. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, higher German growth alongside eurozone inflation above 3% in 2026 and 2027 points to a recovery taking place while costs stay high, and a forecast of slowing German growth towards 2028 suggests the recovery is not expected to broaden. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, German demand from manufacturing and construction customers depends on volumes and investment more than on headline growth, and eurozone inflation of this level keeps pressure on raw material, energy and labour costs. Points that may be worth considering include German industrial orders and output, eurozone inflation data and the Commission's country chapters.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | MarketScreener | People's Daily

item.title: US private data-centre construction spending rose 90% year on year in September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of USD 96.5 billion, 12.2% of private non-residential construction spending, Allianz Trade reports.
item.description:
Private data-centre construction spending in the US rose 90% year on year in September, reaching a seasonally adjusted annual rate of USD 96.5 billion, according to the latest report from Allianz Trade, Commercial Times reports. Data centres accounted for 12.2% of private non-residential construction spending. The market consensus expects US data-centre construction spending to increase 33% in 2026 and 25% in 2027. In the same month, private power construction spending rose 12.1% year on year, driven by power generation and grid investment. The row does not give the number or size of projects, a regional split, or how much of the increase reflects higher construction prices rather than more building.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives spending values for one month at an annual rate, not built floor area or volumes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a segment that now takes about one dollar in eight of private non-residential construction spending, with power and grid investment rising beside it, may act as a demand driver that could offset any weaker segments of commercial building. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, data centres and power infrastructure use flooring, sealing, fire-protection, insulation and thermal management materials, so the growth of this segment shifts where construction and electronics demand for these products arises. Points that may be worth considering include the next monthly construction data, local restrictions on data-centre building and the split between buildings and equipment.

Commercial Times
